justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift assumption from what I inferred to be a current price around $108–109. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of $108.9 essentially anchors near the prevailing price with minimal expected movement, consistent with typical daily volatility in equity or index instruments. At one week, I nudged the estimate slightly higher to $109.5, reflecting a small positive drift that tends to characterize broad market instruments over short horizons in the absence of strong contrary signals. At one month, the estimate rises further to $110.5, extrapolating that gentle drift over a longer period while acknowledging that mean reversion forces and macro headwinds could easily offset it. In all cases, the drift assumption is modest because I had no strong directional signal to justify a more aggressive forecast.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated to reflect realistic historical volatility scaling with the square root of time. At one day, the interval is relatively tight ($105.8–$111.9), reflecting typical intraday-to-overnight price ranges. At one week, the band widens to roughly ±6 points, consistent with weekly realized volatility for many equity instruments. At one month, the band expands substantially to ±12–13 points around the central estimate, capturing the compounding uncertainty over approximately 20 trading days. These widths implicitly assume volatility in a moderate regime — not a crisis period but not an unusually calm one either.

Several risks could push outcomes outside the stated intervals. On the upside, a surprisingly strong macroeconomic data release, a dovish policy pivot by a major central bank, or a significant corporate earnings beat could drive prices well above $123 at the one-month horizon. On the downside, a geopolitical shock, an unexpected credit event, a hot inflation print triggering rate-hike fears, or a sudden liquidity crunch could easily breach the $98 lower bound. Structural market breaks — think flash crashes or circuit-breaker events — are low-probability but fat-tail risks that my intervals do not fully price in.

Finally, it is worth noting that my forecasts were generated without real-time data, so if conditions had already shifted materially before the forecast was anchored, the intervals could be systematically miscalibrated. Model uncertainty itself — the possibility that the underlying price process has changed regime — is an additional source of risk that is difficult to quantify but should lead a thoughtful reader to treat even the one-month confidence interval as optimistic about coverage, perhaps warranting an additional 10–15% buffer on each side to feel truly conservative.
